title: Mechanisms & Kinematics Analysis
summary: Degrees of freedom, Grashof and four-bar classification, slider-crank kinematics, and cam follower motion programs.

sections.heading: Machines as Constrained Motion
sections.content: A **mechanism** converts input motion (rotation, linear stroke) into a desired output motion using links, joints, and a fixed frame. Kinematics analysis answers *where and how fast things move* — the geometry of motion, independent of forces. The same mechanism family — the four-bar, the slider-crank, the cam — appears in engines, robots, presses, and feeders, so mastering these few archetypes covers most of industrial machinery.

sections.heading: Degrees of Freedom (Gruebler)
sections.content:
The **mobility** of a planar mechanism — how many independent inputs it needs — is given by the Gruebler/Kutzbach equation:

$$DOF = 3(L-1) - 2J_1 - J_2$$

with $L$ links (including ground), $J_1$ one-dof joints (pins, sliders), $J_2$ two-dof joints (rolling contact). Examples:

- **Four-bar**: $3(4-1) - 2(4) - 0 = 1$ → one input (the crank) fully determines the motion.
- **Slider-crank**: 4 links, 4 one-dof joints (3 pins + 1 slider) → $DOF = 1$.
- A **double-parallelogram** (e.g. some suspension linkages): $DOF = 2$ — the classic "overconstrained but intended" case that needs the designer to notice the second freedom.

If $DOF < 1$ the mechanism is locked (a structure); if > 1, it needs more actuators or it flops. Special cases (three collinear joints, coincident links) give the equation wrong answers — always sanity-check by hand.

sections.heading: Four-Bar: Grashof & Classification
sections.content:
The four-bar linkage (ground, crank, coupler, rocker) is the workhorse of mechanisms. Its behavior is decided by the **Grashof condition**:

$$s + l \leq p + q$$

($s$ shortest link, $l$ longest, $p$, $q$ the other two). Grashof linkages have continuous rotation of the shortest link; non-Grashof linkages only rock.

Example — links 2, 7, 5, 6 mm: $s + l = 2 + 7 = 9 \leq p + q = 5 + 6 = 11$ → **Grashof**. The shortest link (2 mm) can rotate fully, and the mechanism is a:

- **Crank-rocker** if the ground is fixed to a link adjacent to the shortest (input crank rotates, output rocks);
- **Double-crank** if ground is the shortest link (both side links rotate fully);
- **Double-rocker** if ground is opposite the shortest (everything rocks, coupling only).

Applications: crank-rocker = the classic "(rocker) output rocker" — pump linkages, windshield wipers; double-crank = drag-link feed mechanisms; the **quick-return** family gives a slow power stroke and fast return stroke by geometry alone — a 3:1 time ratio comes free with the right proportions.

sections.heading: Slider-Crank Kinematics
sections.content:
The **slider-crank** (crank, connecting rod, slider) converts rotation to reciprocation — the heart of IC engines, piston pumps, and presses. The piston position from crank angle:

$$x = r\cos\theta + l\sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{r}{l}\sin\theta\right)^2}$$

Example — crank $r = 50$ mm, rod $l = 200$ mm, at $\theta = 45°$:

$$x = 50 \times 0.7071 + 200\sqrt{1 - (0.25 \times 0.7071)^2} = 35.4 + 200 \times 0.9843 = 232.2 \text{ mm}$$

The velocity of the slider is **not** sinusoidal — dwell near the crank dead centers and acceleration spikes near stroke ends are geometry, not control error. Short connecting rods relative to crank ($r/l$ ~ 1/4 typical, 1/3 aggressive) give larger strokes but harsher acceleration; engine rod ratios ~3.0–4.0 balance this against piston side thrust and height.

sections.heading: Cam-Follower Motion Programs
sections.content:
A **cam** generates a prescribed output motion from continuous rotation: the follower profile traces the cam surface. The motion program is the design decision — follower displacement, velocity, acceleration vs cam angle:

- **Constant velocity** — sharp acceleration impulses at the transitions: usable at slow speed only (worst dynamic behavior).
- **Simple harmonic motion (SHM)** — smooth velocity, but acceleration spikes at start/stop: moderate speeds.
- **Cycloidal** — displacement $y = h\left(\frac{\theta}{\beta} - \frac{1}{2\pi}\sin\frac{2\pi\theta}{\beta}\right)$ — zero acceleration at start AND end, continuous throughout: the standard for high-speed cams.

Follower types: flat-faced (needs positive offset; good for force), roller (low friction, industry standard), knife (cheap, wears). Check the **pressure angle** — the angle between cam normal and follower direction; above ~30° the follower side-loads its guide and jams. Re-profile the cam or enlarge the base circle when the pressure angle fails.

sections.heading: From Kinematics to Machines
sections.content:
Mechanism analysis is the skeleton under machine design:

- **Quick-return mechanisms** (Whitworth, crank-shaper) convert a uniform input rotation into an uneven output stroke — used in shapers and indexing machines to spend more time on the cutting stroke.
- **Geneva mechanisms** convert continuous rotation into indexed partial turns with smooth engagement — the classic film projector and rotary-table indexer.
- **Toggle mechanisms** (linkages near dead-center) multiply force enormously near lockup — used in clamps and presses precisely where motion nearly stops.
- **Four-bar dwell approximations** give near-stationary output for part of the cycle without a cam — cheaper in production than cam profiles.

The design loop closes with **forces**: once velocities and accelerations are known, the required torques and joint reactions follow from Newton's laws — feeding directly into the [[bearings-and-shafts|bearing]] and [[fatigue-and-failure-analysis|fatigue]] sizing of every link.

keyTakeaways: Mobility DOF = 3(L−1) − 2J1 − J2; one dof = one input per mechanism.
Grashof (s + l ≤ p + q) decides whether a four-bar has continuous rotation — and which type it is.
Slider-crank motion is non-sinusoidal; acceleration spikes near dead centers are geometric.
Cycloidal cam profiles run smoothest at speed; keep pressure angle under ~30°.
